\paragraph{Model Collapse in Recursive Training.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024} provided the first systematic empirical study of model collapse, showing that iteratively training on self-generated data leads to progressive loss of distributional tails.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{strong_collapse2025} formalized this phenomenon theoretically, proving that collapse occurs even under optimal retraining conditions.
Subsequent work has characterized collapse through an information-theoretic lens~\cite{entropy_collapse2025}, demonstrating monotonic entropy decrease across generations.
A critical gap remains: existing analyses are post-hoc diagnostics, offering no mechanism for online detection or intervention during training.

\paragraph{Spectral Monitoring of Representations.}
Garrido et al.~\cite{rankme2023} introduced RankMe, showing that the effective rank of representation matrices correlates strongly with downstream task performance without requiring labeled evaluation.
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} extended spectral analysis to monitor training dynamics, identifying phase transitions in learned representations.
These works establish spectral health as a reliable, low-cost proxy for representation quality---a property we exploit as our control signal.

\paragraph{Static Data Mixing Strategies.}
He et al.~\cite{he2025golden} proposed a fixed ``golden ratio'' for synthetic-to-real mixing that minimizes degradation under i.i.d.\ assumptions.
Garg et al.~\cite{garg2025} provided theoretical bounds on optimal mixing proportions as a function of distribution shift.
Further empirical studies~\cite{mixing2026} have validated that even small real-data fractions substantially slow collapse.
However, all these approaches prescribe a \emph{static} ratio, ignoring the temporal dynamics: early generations may need less real data (representations still healthy), while later generations facing accelerating collapse require more.

\paragraph{Data Accumulation and Recursive Stability.}
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024} showed that accumulating all past real and synthetic data avoids collapse, but this treats the real/synthetic ratio as static and is inapplicable under fixed budget constraints where total real data is bounded.
Recursive stability theory~\cite{recursive_stability2025} proves that maintaining a constant real-data proportion ensures convergence in self-consuming loops, motivating the optimization of that proportion adaptively rather than fixing it a priori.
Falahati et al.~\cite{falahati2026} demonstrated that pluralistic reward curation prevents collapse even without ratio control, offering a complementary mechanism to mixing-ratio adaptation.
Data Mixing Laws~\cite{data_mixing_laws2024} optimize data mixtures by predicting language modeling performance from mixture composition, but do not address spectral health signals or synthetic-data collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Adaptive Data Selection.}
DCES~\cite{dces2026} uses intra-cluster dispersion to adaptively rebalance center-edge sampling ratios within the synthetic pool, tested on GPT-2, Qwen, and OPT-6.7B across 10 rounds. Key distinction: DCES adapts sample selection \emph{within} the synthetic data, while we adapt the global real/synthetic mixing ratio based on spectral health.
ADAPT~\cite{adapt2025} uses meta-gradients to learn task sampling proportions under explicit token budgets for multi-task instruction tuning. It demonstrates budget-constrained adaptive allocation but addresses multi-task domain mixing rather than real/synthetic collapse prevention.

\paragraph{Calibration and Knowledge Preservation.}
Recent work has monitored calibration drift~\cite{calibration2025} and knowledge collapse~\cite{knowledge_collapse2025} as complementary degradation signals.
Whether spectral indicators or calibration metrics provide earlier warning of collapse remains an open empirical question that our experiments aim to investigate.
Our contribution is the first method to close the loop: using a spectral early-warning signal to drive \emph{budget-constrained temporal allocation} of real data across recursive training generations.

**Title:** Characterizing Model Behavior Under Synthetic Data Training: An Empirical Study Across Scales and Mixing Ratios

**Authors:** Y. Du, G. Wu, G. Tang, W. Wang, Q. Fan (and 4 other authors, as noted in the paper)

**Overview:** The paper presents a controlled empirical study examining model performance, calibration, and output characteristics when trained on varying synthetic-to-external data ratios, using the Pythia model suite (410M-12B parameters) across five diverse tasks, with models evaluated after one to three training iterations with synthetic data proportions ranging from 0-50%.

**Key Findings:** Models maintain stable performance with up to 20% synthetic data, but degradation accelerates beyond 30%; larger models (6.9B-12B) show greater robustness to synthetic data than smaller models (410M-1.4B); calibration degradation precedes accuracy loss, providing an early warning signal; and task characteristics matter, with reasoning tasks degrading faster than retrieval tasks under synthetic data training.

The paper was submitted on October 1, 2025.

## DCES: Dynamic Center-Edge Sampling for Model Collapse Mitigation

The paper proposes "DCES" (dynamic center-edge sampling), a dynamic data selection framework to address model collapse in iterative self-training of language models.

### Key Problem

Iterative self-training of language models presents a promising avenue for realizing self-improving Artificial Intelligence systems; however, this process is often hindered by the fundamental challenge of "Model Collapse," where models undergo catastrophic performance degradation and diversity collapse when recursively trained on their own increasingly homogenized synthetic data.

### The DCES Solution

The approach introduces a coupled center/edge processing mechanism that combines diversity injection (token-level editing for center samples) with noise control (anchor-based quality filtering for edge samples), so that the feedback-driven sampling remains effective under noisy synthetic generation.

### Key Innovation

While several individual components in DCES (e.g., K-means, EMA smoothing, probability-based filtering) are based on standard techniques, the core novelty lies in their system-level coupling into a model-aware, dynamic closed-loop data selection mechanism: training-time signals (intra-cluster dispersion) are fed back to continuously rebalance data selection, enabling self-correction under a drifting synthetic data distribution.

### Results

Extensive evaluations across multiple model architectures show that DCES improves robustness to collapse compared to naive self-training baselines (e.g., slower PPL/loss degradation and mitigated entropy collapse), while revealing calibration and semantic-fidelity trade-offs in some settings.

The paper was published in MDPI Electronics in February 2026 and represents an important contribution to addressing the challenge of model collapse in synthetic data generation and self-training scenarios.

Now I'm looking at the foundational work on model collapse. Shumailov et al. first demonstrated empirically that training on self-generated data causes progressive loss of distributional tails, while Dohmatob et al. provided theoretical formalization showing collapse occurs even under optimal conditions. Information-theoretic analyses have characterized this through monotonic entropy decrease across generations. \section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse in Recursive Training.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024} provided the first systematic empirical study of model collapse, showing that iteratively training on self-generated data leads to progressive loss of distributional tails.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{strong_collapse2025} formalized this theoretically, proving that collapse occurs even under optimal retraining conditions.
Subsequent work characterized collapse through an information-theoretic lens~\cite{entropy_collapse2025}, demonstrating monotonic entropy decrease across generations.
A critical gap remains: these analyses are post-hoc diagnostics, offering no mechanism for \emph{online} detection or intervention during training.

\paragraph{Spectral Monitoring of Representations.}
Building on the need for online signals, Garrido et al.~\cite{rankme2023} introduced RankMe, showing that the effective rank of representation matrices correlates strongly with downstream performance without requiring labeled evaluation.
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} extended spectral analysis to monitor training dynamics, identifying phase transitions in learned representations.
These works establish spectral health as a reliable, low-cost proxy for representation quality, yet neither closes the loop by using spectral signals to \emph{drive} corrective action.

\paragraph{Static Data Mixing Strategies.}
One natural corrective is mixing real data into synthetic training.
He et al.~\cite{he2025golden} proposed a fixed ``golden ratio'' for synthetic-to-real mixing that minimizes degradation under i.i.d.\ assumptions.
Garg et al.~\cite{garg2025} provided theoretical bounds on optimal proportions as a function of distribution shift, and further empirical work~\cite{mixing2026} validated that even small real-data fractions substantially slow collapse.

\paragraph{Data Accumulation and Adaptive Selection.}
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024} showed that accumulating all past data avoids collapse, but the approach is inapplicable under fixed budget constraints.
Recursive stability theory~\cite{recursive_stability2025} proves that a constant real-data proportion ensures convergence, motivating adaptive optimization of that proportion rather than fixing it a priori.

Complementary work has monitored calibration drift~\cite{calibration2025} and knowledge collapse~\cite{knowledge_collapse2025} as degradation signals orthogonal to spectral indicators.
